Hatchlings of Darevskia uzzelli emerge from their parchment-shelled eggs with a snout–vent length of approximately 2.25 cm [Lb = approximately 2.25 cm], a value derived from comparative data on the closely related Darevskia derjugini. This modest size at eclosion reflects the limited yolk reserves available to the lecithotrophic larva during its development within the cleidoic egg. Upon emergence, these young-of-year reptiles are fully independent and begin foraging for small arthropods within the rocky crevices of their montane habitats. The neonatal body mass at this stage averages only 0.26 grams [Wwb = 0.26 grams], a figure likewise inferred from Darevskia derjugini, which underscores the energetic constraints faced by the newly emerged offspring. Field observations indicate that the initial weeks of exogenous feeding are critical for rapid growth, as individuals must accumulate sufficient somatic resources to survive their first winter dormancy period.

Adult females of Darevskia uzzelli ultimately achieve a maximum snout–vent length of 6.7 cm [Li = 6.7 cm], a dimension that places them among the smaller-bodied members of the genus. The corresponding ultimate wet body mass for these reproductively active adults is 5.12 grams [Wwi = 5.12 grams], a value consistent with the slender, saxicolous morphology typical of rock-dwelling lacertids. Gravid individuals exhibit a noticeable abdominal distension as the clutch of developing yolked eggs occupies a substantial fraction of the coelomic cavity. This comparatively small adult body size suggests a life-history strategy oriented toward early reproduction and relatively high reproductive effort per season, a pattern frequently observed in lacertid lizards inhabiting climatically unpredictable environments. Body condition indices calculated from field-captured females indicate that mass fluctuates considerably across the active season, peaking just prior to oviposition and declining thereafter as energy reserves are depleted.

Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a constant 20 °C [T = 20 °C], the maximum reproductive rate for Darevskia uzzelli has been estimated from the product of clutch size and clutch frequency. Females deposit a single clutch of eight eggs each year [Ri = eight eggs each year], with a reproductive frequency of one clutch per year [F_R_i = one clutch per year]. This annual reproductive output, implying a daily egg production of eight eggs per 365 days, is modest compared to some congeners but appears to be constrained by the short active season characteristic of the species' high-elevation habitat. The parchment-shelled eggs are typically buried beneath loose rock slabs, where the stable thermal microenvironment presumably facilitates successful embryonic development. The decision to produce a single, relatively large clutch rather than multiple smaller clutches across the season likely reflects a bet-hedging strategy to maximise offspring survival in a variable thermal regime.

When maintained at a constant 20 °C [T = 20 °C], longevity in Darevskia uzzelli has been documented at an estimated lifespan of six years [am = six years], based on captive-rearing studies conducted under standard vivarium conditions. This maximum recorded longevity, equivalent to approximately 2190 days, is typical for a lacertid of this size and suggests a relatively slow pace of life compared to lowland congeners. Pre-reproductive juveniles and sub-adults face high annual mortality rates, with predation by birds and snakes representing the primary cause of extrinsic mortality. Older individuals exhibit signs of reproductive senescence, including reduced clutch viability and lower hatching success, particularly in females beyond their fourth reproductive season. The interplay between this relatively short lifespan and the single-clutch annual reproductive output suggests that individual females have only a handful of breeding opportunities across their lifetime, placing a premium on the success of each reproductive event.

At a constant 20 °C [T = 20 °C], first reproduction in Darevskia uzzelli occurs at three years after hatching [tR = three years after hatching], indicating that females require approximately 1095 days post-hatching to attain sufficient body size and energy reserves for their first successful clutch. This delay before the first breeding event corresponds to a period of sustained somatic growth during the juvenile and sub-adult stages. Sexual maturation, as evidenced by the onset of gonadal activity and the production of vitellogenic follicles, occurs slightly earlier, but the first successful oviposition is typically deferred until the third active season. The age at first reproduction is relatively late for a lizard of this size, a trait that may be linked to the energetic demands of reaching the 5.12 grams necessary to support a full clutch. Comparative data from other Darevskia species suggest that altitudinal variation in thermal regime can shift this timing, with populations from cooler sites tending to delay reproduction further.
